blindSummary:
This country has a strong legal framework — a gender identity law allowing self-determination (2019, no medical requirements), marriage equality (2022), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (2012), and a positive prison-service protocol that places trans inmates in facilities matching their gender identity and provides healthcare examination on entry. A UN human-rights committee commended the country's police measures to promote LGBTIQ rights.

But 2024 was a year of regression — the first rollback since democracy returned in 1990 — with legislators rejecting non-discrimination-law reforms and the main national LGBT organisation's 2025 annual report describing a "breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus" on LGBTIQ+ rights. Documented violence includes a trans person murdered and dismembered (described as the country's biggest hate crime), a transphobic hotel attack in the capital (beating, captivity, death threats), and institutional discrimination against the country's first trans police officer.

The country's top court restored a femicide conviction for the murder of a trans woman (overturning an appeals-court ruling that she did not "legally qualify" as a woman). For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, the capital welcoming.
blindOutOfScope: General crime (theft, scams) and earthquake risk affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law includes SOGI as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition law passed 2019; third-sex option for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006; non-binding intersex-affirming health guidance (2023) recommends against unnecessary surgeries; in 2025 a court issued the country's first lesbophobic femicide conviction.

NOTE: the main national LGBT organisation's 24th annual human-rights report on sexual and gender diversity (2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).
Investigative outlet (Jan 2024): profile of a young trans man murdered and dismembered in 2023 - described as the country's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed.

National TV network (Sept 2021): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a hotel in the capital in a transphobic attack; the victim recounts fearing for his life.

National daily: the country's prison service signed a new protocol for trans inmates - placement according to gender identity, segmented housing, medical examination on entry to determine hormonal/surgical treatment needs, and respect for assumed-gender expression.
International survey group's country profile for this country: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a dedicated transgender-rights barometer index.

Foreign newspaper (April 2025): the country's first trans police officer sued the national police for discrimination - relegated to administrative tasks, private life exposed without consent, denied support against online hate, and transition-related surgery refused.

Main national LGBT organisation's achievements page: lists the organisation's historical milestones across legal, judicial, public-policy, human-rights, mobilisation and international sectors benefiting lesbians, gays, bisexuals and trans people in this country - institutional-culture context.
blindLocalsOnly: The self-determination gender identity law and the prison-service inmate protocol are resident-facing; the trans police officer case and prison healthcare provisions concern residents.
blindTangential: Marriage equality since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
